title: Act III, Scene III
focus: Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell

teacherSummary.text: Romeo hides in the Friar's cell, despairing at banishment. The Nurse arrives; Romeo draws a dagger to kill himself; the Friar stops him and lays out a plan: spend the night with Juliet, flee to Mantua, and wait until the marriage can be announced.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act III, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act III, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act III, Scene III develops the idea of Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and diction / vocabulary shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act III, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act III, Scene III suggests about Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act III, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act III, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act III, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene III and its treatment of Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Romeo's despair in the Friar's cell. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “O Lord, I could have stay’d here all the night / To hear good counsel: O, what learning is! / My lord, I’ll” (Act III, Scene III, Nurse (speech 33)).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: O Lord, I could have stay’d here all the night / To hear good counsel: O, what learning is! / My lord, I’ll

symbolsAndMotifs.name: fate and the stars
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: From "star-cross'd" in the Prologue to Romeo's "I defy you, stars," the lovers feel steered by fortune, while the plot shows human choices and accidents. In this scene: “Tis torture, and not mercy: heaven is here, / Where Juliet lives; and every cat and dog / And” (Act III, Scene III, Romeo (speech 10)).

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Romeo draws a dagger to kill himself and the Friar stops him. Use the safe-messaging script; focus on the Friar's reasons for hope and on who Romeo could turn to.
contentNotes.studentPreview: In this scene a character tries to take his own life and is stopped. Support is available if this is hard to read.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “What does the Friar say to give Romeo reasons to live?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
safeMessaging.studentResource: If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.
safeMessaging.counselorPrompt: Let a counselor know in advance that this scene is being taught.
